title: OpenMHC: Accelerating the Science of Wearable Foundation Models
claim: A large, richly structured dataset spans many participants, sensor channels and tasks, and supports benchmarking of diverse models.
layout: Stat banner on top, three panels: timeline plots above, dot plot below
description: The figure opens with a banner of ten large headline numbers in two rows: 11.9K participants, 3 countries, 92 device models, 2.8M participant-days, 67M wear-hours, 19 channels, 170 linked variables and 32 predictive tasks. Panel (a), at left, shows one participant-day as stacked minute-level sensor traces. The traces are grouped and colored by Activity (blue), Physiology (orange), Sleep (purple) and Workout (green). Next to them, small horizontal bars give the number of users and user-days for each channel. Panel (b), at right, is a blue timeline of all 11,894 participants, sorted by start date, running from 2014 to 2026. Panel (c) spans the bottom. It is a dot plot of skill scores versus a linear baseline for five models across about 25 tasks. The tasks are grouped into five color-bracketed health domains, with bold domain summaries marked by asterisks.
caption: The OPENMHC dataset at a glance. 11,894 participants across 3 countries (US, UK, HK), 50 US states plus DC, and 92 device models, contributing 2.82M participant-days (over 67M participant-hours) of minute-level sensor data over a 13-year calendar span (earliest to latest recorded day), alongside 170 linked self-report and sparse HealthKit variables and 32 predictive tasks. (a) Example of minute-level wearable data participant-day for one user as a 19×1,440 matrix spanning Activity, Watch-derived Physiology, Sleep, and 10 Workout types (combined into a single channel for this visualization). Right columns report cohort-wide coverage: number of users contributing to the channel and total user-days. (b) Participation timeline: each line is one of the 11,894 participants, sorted by enrollment date, spanning their first to last contributed day. (c) Skill Scores (S, % vs. Linear baseline) for selected predictive tasks, grouped into five health domains (Demographics, Medical Conditions, Vitals & Biomarkers, Mental Well-being, Sleep & Lifestyle), for five methods: MULTIROCKET, XGBOOST, WBM, LSM-2, and CHRONOS-2. Overall and per-domain summary scores are marked with ∗.
abstract: Mobile and wearable devices offer an unprecedented opportunity for continuous, passive health monitoring and active health coaching. However, the largest wearable datasets are proprietary, and leading wearable foundation models trained on them are rarely open weight or include reproducible training code. To accelerate open science in wearable health, we introduce OpenMyHeartCounts (OpenMHC), the largest and most comprehensive wearable health dataset broadly accessible to qualified researchers, alongside open-source implementations and weights for recent wearable foundation models. Derived from over a decade of data collected through the My Heart Counts study app, OpenMHC comprises over 67M participant-hours of wearable recordings across up to 19 sensor channels (e.g., step count, heart rate, sleep, workouts) and up to 170 health, lifestyle, mood, and behavioral variables from 11,894 participants. Furthermore, we establish a benchmark for standardized evaluation across three tasks: (1) health and behavioral outcome prediction, (2) multivariate data imputation, and (3) time-series forecasting. Benchmarking classical methods alongside recent wearable and time-series foundation models, we find that while foundation models perform strongly, carefully tuned classical baselines like XGBoost remain highly competitive. By uniting broad-access wearable data with open code and model weights, OpenMHC provides a framework needed to drive reproducible advances in wearable health AI.
